- **Plurals.** The vocabulary carries singular words only; matching `LONGBOWS` is `ah-bn6.2`'s job,
  by trying `item_spellings`' three spellings against this set.
- **`order_commands`.** It stays exactly as it is; the completion popup keeps using it.
- **`coreVocabulary.generated.ts`** and its generator `crates/core/tests/generated_ts.rs`. The
  ruleset half of this vocabulary is runtime data, so none of it belongs in a compiled-in list.
- **Buildings.** `Ruleset.buildings` exists, but no order argument names a building type; leave it
  out rather than uppercasing words the grammar never expects.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core          # the vocabulary's own tests
pnpm run check:fast                      # lint, typecheck, unit + tooling suites, fmt, clippy
```

The tooling suite inside `check:fast` is what catches a half-wired boundary. By hand, nothing to
look at — this bead has no visible surface. Sanity check in a node REPL or a scratch test if
wanted: `client.orderVocabulary(rulesetJson)` returns a sorted uppercase list containing `MOVE`,
`ALL`, `NW`, `SILV` and a skill word from the committed ruleset.

## Known traps

- **`expect(renames.size).toBe(26)`** at `scripts/tauriCommands.test.ts` is a hard-coded count of
  Tauri commands. It must become `27`, and the failure it gives when you forget reads as an
  unrelated arithmetic mismatch.
- **`Arg::Rest(inner)` yields nothing from `grammar::keywords`** (`grammar.rs:530-535`). Recurse
  into it yourself or every repeated argument's keywords vanish silently — no test but the one named
  above will notice.
- **`grammar::keywords` is `pub(super)`.** A sibling module inside `orders` can call it; anything
  outside `orders` cannot. Put the new function in `orders/`, and do not widen the visibility to
  work around a misplaced file.
- **Parse the ruleset through `cache::with_global`**, as `command_order_argument_completions`
  (`:472-476`) and the wasm twin do — a direct `serde_json::from_str` reparses a ruleset the cache
  already holds, on every keystroke once `ah-bn6.2` lands.
- **The `TAURI_COMMANDS` row's keys are the Rust parameter names, in declaration order.** A
  mismatch is caught by `commandParameters` in the lockstep test, whose message names the command
  but not the offending key.
- **`fakeAdapter` in `packages/core-client/src/index.test.ts:30` is typed against `CoreAdapter`**
  on purpose, so adding a method breaks that file's compile. That is the design, not an accident —
  fill it in rather than loosening the type.
- **ts-rs codegen is driven by `cargo test`** and `scripts/checkGenerated.ts` fails a stale
  `packages/core-client/src/generated/`. Nothing here adds a `#[derive(TS)]` type — `Vec<String>`
  crosses as a plain array — so no regeneration should be needed; if `check:generated` complains,
  something grew a derive it did not need.

title: Drop the 'spoils' line from the battle chooser
description: Every battle in the battle dialog's left-hand chooser ends with a line reading `spoils` (`BattlesDialog.tsx:163`): {summary.hasSpoils ? spoils : null} The right-hand pane already shows what the spoils were, properly labelled and valued (`BattlesDialog.tsx:247-250`). So the word in the chooser tells the reader nothing they cannot see better one pane over, and it makes every battle in the list look the same as every other. **The request:** remove it. Spoils are shown on the right. ## Small, and worth checking two things - **`hasSpoils` may become unused.** If nothing else reads it, the summary can drop it too rather than leaving a field computed for a removed line. - **The chooser rows may lose their shape.** The line was presumably contributing to each row's height or rhythm; removing it should leave the list looking deliberate rather than clipped. ## Validation The chooser lists battles with no `spoils` line. A battle with spoils still shows them in full in the right-hand pane, and one without still shows nothing there.
design: ## Context Every battle in the battle dialog's left-hand chooser ends with the word `spoils`: ```tsx // packages/shared/src/workspace/BattlesDialog.tsx:163 {summary.hasSpoils ? spoils : null} ``` The right-hand pane already shows what the spoils were, properly labelled and valued (`BattlesDialog.tsx:247-250`), so the word in the chooser tells the reader nothing they cannot see better one pane over — and it makes every battle in the list look the same as every other. The navigator asked for it to go. **One correction to the bead**, which matters for what to expect afterwards: `spoils` is not a line of its own. It is one chip in a wrapped row — `` (line 151) — beside the hex, the attacker's losses and the defender's. Removing it takes a chip out of a flex row, so the row's height and rhythm are unaffected and there is no gap to close. The bead's worry about the rows "losing their shape" does not arise; what changes is that a battle with spoils and one without now read identically in the chooser, which is the point. ## Files to change, and what to reuse ### `packages/shared/src/workspace/BattlesDialog.tsx` Line 163 goes. Nothing else in that component changes — the hex, the attacker's losses and the defender's stay exactly as they are, and `BattleDetail`'s spoils section (lines 247–250) is untouched and is where spoils are read from now on. ### `packages/shared/src/workspace/battles.ts` `hasSpoils` has **exactly one non-test reader**, the line being removed (`git grep -n "hasSpoils" packages` returns `BattlesDialog.tsx:163`, `battles.ts:30`, `battles.ts:58` and three test assertions). So it goes with it: - the field on the summary type (line 30); - its computation, `hasSpoils: battle.spoils !== null` (line 58). A field computed for a removed line is a field the next reader has to work out the purpose of, and this one's purpose is now nothing. ### `packages/shared/src/workspace/battles.test.ts` The three `expect(summary.hasSpoils)` assertions (lines 42, 48, 75) go with the field. **Read what else each of those tests asserts before deleting a line** — if a test exists only for `hasSpoils` it goes whole; if it also pins the losses or the hex, only the one assertion goes. ## Increments One. RED: delete the three assertions and the field; the component no longer compiles at line 163. GREEN: delete line 163. Done in that order the compiler names the site for you, which is the whole safety net a change this size needs. ## The test plan No new tests. What matters is what survives: | Test | File | What it pins | |---|---|---| | (existing) the chooser's rows | `BattlesDialog.test.tsx` | Still list every battle with its hex and both losses. **If any test asserts the word `spoils` in the chooser, it goes** — it pins the behaviour being removed | | (existing) the detail pane's spoils | same | Unchanged: a battle with spoils still shows them in full, one without still shows nothing | | (existing) `battles.test.ts` | same | Everything except the three `hasSpoils` assertions | Suites: `pnpm -r run test`, inside `pnpm run check:fast`. No browser suite — but check `tests/smoke/` for the word before finishing (`git grep -n "spoils" tests/`), because a smoke walk asserting it in the chooser would go red on CI rather than locally. ## User-facing decisions **One, already taken**: the navigator asked for the chip to be removed, on the grounds that the right-hand pane says it better. Nothing else about the dialog changes — not the chooser's other chips, not the detail pane, not the order of the list. Nothing to ask, and nothing to mock up: this bead removes a word. ## Out of scope - **The detail pane's spoils section** (lines 247–250), which is where spoils are shown and stays exactly as it is. - **`Battle.spoils` in the core**, still read by the detail pane. - **The chooser's other chips** — hex, attacker losses, defender losses. - **Any other tidy-up in this dialog.** If removing this one makes something else look wrong, say so and file it; do not fix it here. ## Validation ```bash pnpm run check:fast ``` Then look at it: open the battles dialog on a turn with several battles, at least one with spoils. The chooser shows the hex and the losses and no `spoils`; selecting the battle with spoils still shows them, valued, on the right. ## Known traps - **Delete the field, not just its use.** `hasSpoils` would otherwise sit on the summary type with nothing reading it — the smell Forge files beads about, and this bead is the moment it is free to remove. - **`git grep -n "spoils" tests/`** before finishing. A Playwright walk asserting the chooser's word fails on CI, not on `check:fast`, which is the slowest possible way to find out. - **The row is a wrapped flex of chips, not a stack of lines.** Do not "close the gap" left behind — there is not one, and `gap-2` handles the spacing.
acceptance_criteria: The battle chooser in the left-hand pane shows no spoils line. The right-hand pane still shows a battle's spoils when it has them, unchanged. No field is left computed solely for the removed line.

title: Selecting an arriving unit draws the route bringing it here
description:
Selecting a unit that has just arrived in a hex says nothing about where it came from. The map already
knows how to draw a path across hexes — `RouteOverlay` and `routeSegments` do it for planned routes,
read against the ground they cross — so the display machinery exists; what is missing is pointing it
at an arrival rather than a plan.

**The request:** selecting an arriving unit shows its movement on the map, so its origin is visible.
**For ships, that must include passengers, not only the sailors.**

## The part to establish first

Where the origin comes from. Candidates, and they are not equivalent:

- **The previous turn's report.** The client already holds consecutive turns and can diff them
  (`ah-jg6.*`), so a unit present in both says where it was — this gives the endpoints but not the
  path between them.
- **The unit's own orders.** A `MOVE` or `SAIL` from the previous turn is the path, hex by hex, and is
  what the player actually wrote.
- **The report's events.** Worth checking what they record about movement; the sample turn's events
  are mostly gives and rewards.

Endpoints alone may be enough to answer "where did this come from"; the full path is what makes it a
tracker. Which is available decides the shape of the whole bead.

## Ships are the point, not an edge case

A passenger aboard a ship issues no movement order of its own — the ship moves and it goes along. So
any approach built on "read this unit's movement order" answers nothing for exactly the units a player
is most confused about. A passenger's origin is its ship's origin, which means the feature has to
know a unit is aboard and whose voyage to attribute to it.

## For the planner to settle with the navigator

- Which source of origin, per above, and whether endpoints-only is acceptable for a first version.
- **How it is drawn**, and how it differs from a planned route — the map already uses that language
  for something else, and two kinds of line meaning opposite things (where it went, where it will go)
  would be worse than none.
- Whether it appears on selection or needs asking for. Automatic is what was requested; it also means
  the map redraws on every selection.
- Units that did not move, and units seen for the first time — neither has an origin to show.

## Validation

Select a unit that walked in from a neighbouring hex: its movement is visible and correct. Select a
passenger that arrived aboard a ship: the same voyage is shown for it as for the ship's crew. Select
a unit that did not move: nothing misleading appears.
design:
## Context

**The bead's original description was about history — where a unit came from last turn. That is not
what was wanted, and the navigator corrected it during planning (2026-08-17).** What is wanted is
about *this* turn's preview, seen from the other end:

> In turn 25, Unit A and B are on a ship and unit A issues `SAIL S`. If I select either unit in their
> current hex, I can see that they are leaving — the unit list says so and the map shows the sail
> path. Now if I go to the hex to the south, their destination, I can see both units there as
> arriving units. But when I select them, I want to see the path they will be sailing to reach this
> hex.

So: **no history, no previous turn, no new kind of line.** The existing route overlay, from the
existing this-turn trace, drawn when an arriving unit is selected in the hex it is arriving at.

## Why nothing is drawn today

You can *see* the arriving units because `UnitTableDock` is given both the hex and its preview slice
and merges them (`AppShell.tsx:2922`, `mergePreview` in `packages/shared/src/unitPreview.ts`). But the
shell's own notion of the selected unit reads the **report** only:

```tsx
// packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx:578
const unit = useMemo(
  () => hex?.region?.units.find((candidate) => candidate.unitId === selectedUnitId) ?? null,
  [hex, selectedUnitId]
);
```

An arriving unit is not in the report's units for the destination hex — it is only in the preview — so
`unit` is `null`. Everything downstream then does nothing, correctly and silently:

- the trace effect bails at `!unit?.own` (line 1709) and asks the core for nothing;
- `unitPreview` (line 1982) is null, because it is keyed on `unit`;
- the unit pane has nothing to show.

**And the trace already answers the right question.** `trace_move` starts from the unit's own hex as
the report gives it, so tracing an arriving unit draws the path from its origin to here — precisely
the arrow the navigator asked for — regardless of which hex is selected. Nothing about the drawing
needs to change.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx` — one fallback

`unit` falls back to the hex's preview when the report has no such unit here. `hexPreview` (line 1974)
already holds exactly that slice, and `UnitPreview.unit` is documented as "the full predicted state,
so the row renders exactly like a reported one" — a whole `ReportUnit`, which is what every consumer
of `unit` expects.

```tsx
  /**
   * The selected unit: as the report has it in this hex, or - for a unit that is only arriving here
   * this month - as the preview has it.
   *
   * An arriving unit is in the preview and not in the report, which is why selecting one used to
   * find nothing at all: no trace was asked for and the pane stayed empty, even though the table had
   * just drawn the row that was clicked (ah-0fa). The preview's `unit` is a whole `ReportUnit`, so
   * everything downstream is unchanged.
   */
  const unit = useMemo(
    () =>
      hex?.region?.units.find((candidate) => candidate.unitId === selectedUnitId) ??
      hexPreview?.units.find((previewed) => previewed.unit.unitId === selectedUnitId)?.unit ??
      null,
    [hex, hexPreview, selectedUnitId]
  );
```

**`hexPreview` is declared at line 1974 and `unit` at line 578**, so the memo has to move below it —
or `hexPreview` above. Move `hexPreview` up to just before `unit`: it depends only on `hex` and
`ordersPreview`, both of which are already in scope there, and it keeps the selected-hex derivations
together. Do not reach for a second copy of the lookup.

`unitPreview` (line 1982) then resolves for an arriving unit as well, with no change of its own —
which is what gives the pane its arriving marker for free.

### Nothing else

- **No core change, no wire change.** The trace command, `trace_move`, the preview and the route
  overlay are all untouched.
- **No change to the trace effect** (line 1708). Once `unit` is non-null it runs exactly as it does
  for a unit standing in the selected hex.
- **No change to `UnitTableDock`, `mergePreview`, or the arriving row's rendering.**

### The passenger half is ah-048's

Unit A wrote `SAIL S`, so `readUnitOrders` finds its order and the trace draws. **Unit B, the
passenger, wrote nothing** — so with this bead alone, selecting it in the destination hex fills the
pane but draws no route. `ah-048` is exactly the bead that teaches the core to trace a unit against
the order of the fleet it stands in, and with both merged the navigator's example works for both
units. **This bead is wired to depend on ah-048**, and its own tests cover the ordering unit; the
passenger case is ah-048's test to own.

## Increments

1. **The fallback.** RED: the two `AppShell`-level behaviours below cannot be unit-tested (no DOM in
   this package), so the RED is the smoke test. Move `hexPreview`, add the fallback.
2. **Proof.** The smoke walk below.

## The test plan

`AppShell` has no unit test — `@atlantis/shared` runs vitest in Node with no DOM — so the proof is a
browser walk. Add it beside the existing movement-layer walks:

| Test | File | What it pins |
|---|---|---|
| `selecting an arriving unit in its destination hex draws its route` | `tests/smoke/` (new) | Load `g5f21t24`, write `unit 10575` / `sail se`, select the **destination** hex, select unit 10575 in the units table, and the route overlay is drawn |
| `selecting an arriving unit fills the unit pane` | same walk | The unit panel names the unit, and the row carries the arriving treatment it already has |
| (existing) selecting a unit standing in the selected hex | unchanged | The report path still wins: a unit present in the report is found there, not in the preview |

Suites: `pnpm run check:fast` for the gates, and **`pnpm run test:smoke`**, which is the only thing
that exercises this at all.

## User-facing decisions

Two, the navigator's, 2026-08-17, after they corrected the bead's premise:

1. **Selecting an arriving unit behaves like selecting any other unit** — the map draws the route it
   will take to get here, the unit pane fills. No history, no previous turn, no second style of line.
   *Rejected: folding ah-048's core change into this bead* — one bead that makes both units work, at
   the cost of duplicating work already planned.
2. **The pane shows the unit, marked as arriving**, using the treatment the table's row already
   carries, so it is obvious you are looking at a unit that has not got here yet. *Rejected: showing
   it exactly like any other unit* — nothing would tell you it is not actually here, which the hex's
   own heading contradicts. *Rejected: drawing the route but leaving the pane empty* — selecting
   something and getting an empty pane reads as broken.

**The original bead's questions do not arise** and must not be re-opened: there is no choice of origin
source, no dashed-versus-solid decision, no "units seen for the first time". Those belonged to the
history feature the bead was mistakenly written as. If a history tracker is ever wanted, it is a new
bead.

## Out of scope

- **ah-048**, the passenger's trace, which this depends on.
- **Any use of the previous turn's report or orders.** The whole of this bead is this turn's preview.
- **The route overlay's appearance**, and `chooseRouteOverlay`'s precedence between a plan and a trace.
- **Selecting a unit in a hex it neither occupies nor arrives at.** The fallback is scoped to the
  selected hex's own preview slice, exactly as the report lookup is.
- **Departing rows**, which already work.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke
```

Then the navigator's own example, which Psylocke will repeat: on `neworigins-3.0.0-g5-f21-t24.rep`,
order `unit 10575` / `sail se`. Select the destination hex; both units are listed as arriving. Select
unit 10575 — the map draws the sail path from the northern hex to this one, and the pane shows the
unit. Select unit 10584, the passenger — the same, **once ah-048 has merged**; before then the pane
fills and no route is drawn, which is that bead's job and not a fault in this one.

## Known traps

- **The report must win.** A unit that is genuinely in this hex *and* has a preview row (it changed,
  or it is departing) must resolve to the report's unit, as it does today — the fallback is a `??`
  after it, never a replacement. Getting this backwards would feed every selection a predicted unit
  instead of the reported one.
- **`hexPreview` is declared four hundred lines below `unit`.** Move the declaration, do not
  reimplement the lookup inline; two ways of finding the same slice is how they drift.
- **This is not the bead its description was written as.** The original text is about last turn's
  origin, and the `## Context` above records why it is not that. An implementer following the old
  description would build a history tracker nobody asked for.
- **No DOM in this package.** `check:fast` will pass whether or not this works; the smoke walk is the
  gate.
acceptance_criteria: Selecting a unit that arrived in its hex shows its movement on the map. A unit that travelled as a passenger aboard a ship shows the same voyage as the ship's crew. A unit that did not move, or is seen for the first time, shows nothing misleading. The display is distinguishable from a planned route.

title: STUDY completion offers the skills the unit can actually study
description:
Completing a skill in a `STUDY` order offers the whole skill list. Most of it is unavailable to the
unit doing the studying: wrong kind of unit, dependencies unmet, or already at the level the unit can
reach. The completion will suggest all of it, and the turn fails on whatever the player picked.

**The request:** offer only skills this unit can actually study — allowed for its kind, dependencies
met, and not already at its ceiling.

## Where the pieces are

`order_argument_completions` already takes `unit_id` and `located()` already yields the unit, so
whose skills to reason about is settled. `PRODUCE` already narrows using "this unit's own skills",
which is the closest existing precedent.

What is genuinely new is the eligibility rules, and they come from the ruleset rather than the
report: which skills a unit type may learn, what each skill depends on, and where a unit's ceiling
is. The ruleset is already passed to this function (`rulesetJson`), so the question is what it
actually carries — that is the first thing to establish, and it decides whether this bead is small or
splits in two.

## Worth deciding rather than assuming

- **Which of the three filters are possible now.** If the ruleset carries dependencies but not
  per-type permissions, a partial narrowing is still a large improvement — and better stated than
  quietly incomplete.
- **The ceiling.** A unit at its maximum for a skill genuinely cannot study it further; a unit that
  could with a teacher present is a different case, and the completion should not hide a legitimate
  order.
- **No ruleset loaded.** The signature says only the presence of a ruleset widens the answer, so
  behaviour without one must stay sensible rather than empty.
- **Showing why**, or at least the current level, so a player can tell a skill they have maxed from
  one they never had.
design:
## Context

Completing a skill in a `STUDY` order offers the whole skill list — ninety-six of them. Most are
unavailable to the unit doing the studying, the completion suggests all of it, and the turn fails on
whatever the player picked.

**What the ruleset actually carries was checked before this was planned**, because it decides how much
of the bead is possible. `SkillEntry` (`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:297`) has:

| Field | Use here |
|---|---|
| `cost: Option<i64>` | **Absent means the skill cannot be studied by ordinary means** — the field's own doc says so. A filter, free. |
| `max_level: u32` | How far the skill goes. With the unit's own level, **a filter**. |
| `magic`, `produces`, `cast`, `tag`, `name` | Not eligibility. |

and it carries **no skill dependencies and no per-unit-type permissions**. So of the three filters the
bead names, two are possible today and one is not; and a fourth the bead did not name — skills that
can never be studied at all — is free.

The navigator chose (2026-08-17) to **ship the two and state the rest**, and `ah-6qp` is filed for the
scraper work the other needs.

The mechanism is `ah-84w`'s: `completions_for` (`crates/core/src/orders/completion.rs:139`) already
routes `Arg::Skill` to `skill_completions`, and `located(report, unit_id)` (line 200) already yields
the unit. This is the same shape of change, one function along.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `crates/core/src/orders/completion.rs`

`skill_completions` (line 323) takes the unit and narrows:

```rust
/// What an `Arg::Skill` position offers: the skills this unit could actually study.
///
/// Two filters, and they are the two the ruleset can support:
///
/// - a skill the data page prices nowhere cannot be studied by ordinary means (`SkillEntry::cost`
///   says so in its own doc), so it is never an answer to `STUDY`;
/// - a skill the unit has already taken to the ruleset's maximum cannot be studied further - the
///   same comparison `check_studying` makes for the `study-at-maximum` warning
///   (`semantics.rs`), so the completion and the warning agree by construction.
///
/// Deliberately **not** filtered, because the ruleset carries neither: what a skill depends on, and
/// which kinds of unit may learn it. Both are scraper work, filed as ah-6qp. Until then this list is
/// narrower than it was and wider than it should be, which is the honest state and is better than
/// pretending either way.
///
/// Without a unit - no report, no unit id, or a unit the report does not carry - only the first
/// filter applies: an unstudiable skill is unstudiable for everybody, and the second has nothing to
/// compare against. That keeps the answer sensible rather than empty, which the signature promises
/// (only the presence of a ruleset widens it).
fn skill_completions(ruleset: &Ruleset, unit: Option<&ReportUnit>) -> Vec<OrderCompletion>
```

Body:

```rust
    ruleset
        .skills
        .values()
        .filter(|skill| skill.cost.is_some())
        .filter(|skill| level_of(unit, skill).is_none_or(|level| level < skill.max_level))
        .map(|skill| OrderCompletion {
            value: skill.tag.clone(),
            name: skill.name.clone(),
            detail: detail_for(skill, level_of(unit, skill)),
        })
        .collect()
```

with two small helpers beside it:

```rust
/// The unit's level in this skill, matched case-insensitively as `check_studying` matches it
/// (`semantics.rs`: the report's tags and the ruleset's do not always agree on case).
fn level_of(unit: Option<&ReportUnit>, skill: &SkillEntry) -> Option<u32>;

/// `combat · 45 silver · at 3`, and `combat · 45 silver` for a skill the unit has never studied -
/// absence is the message, and a placeholder on ninety rows says nothing ninety times.
fn detail_for(skill: &SkillEntry, level: Option<u32>) -> String;
```

`cost` is `Some` by the time `detail_for` runs, since the filter above removed the others — so the
`match skill.cost` that exists today collapses to the `Some` arm. Keep the `{cost} silver` wording
exactly.

The call site (line 165) becomes:

```rust
            Arg::Skill if skills.is_empty() => {
                skills = ruleset
                    .map(|ruleset| skill_completions(ruleset, located(report, unit_id).map(|(_, unit)| unit)))
                    .unwrap_or_default();
            }
```

### Nothing else

- **No TypeScript**, no wire change: `detail` is already rendered dimmed beside the label.
- **No change to `item_completions`**, `located`, or the market/produce narrowing.
- **No change to `check_studying`** (`semantics.rs`), which keeps warning about a maxed skill for the
  player who types one by hand. The completion no longer *offers* it; the check still catches it.

## Increments

One. RED: the eight tests below. GREEN: the narrowing, the two helpers, the call site.

## The test plan

| Test | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `study_offers_only_skills_that_can_be_studied` | A skill with `cost: None` never appears — with or without a unit |
| `study_drops_a_skill_the_unit_has_maxed` | Unit at `max_level` in a skill → it is not offered |
| `study_keeps_a_skill_the_unit_can_still_advance` | Unit at `max_level - 1` → offered |
| `study_keeps_a_skill_the_unit_has_never_studied` | No entry on the unit → offered |
| `study_names_the_level_the_unit_has` | `detail` is `combat · 45 silver · at 3`, exactly |
| `study_says_nothing_about_a_level_the_unit_lacks` | `detail` is `combat · 45 silver`, exactly |
| `study_matches_the_unit_skill_tag_whatever_its_case` | The report's case and the ruleset's differ; the level is still found |
| `study_without_a_unit_still_drops_the_unstudiable` | No `unit_id` → the first filter applies, the second does not, and the list is not empty |
| (existing) every `item_completions` test | Unchanged |

Suites: `cargo test --workspace` and `pnpm -r run test`, inside `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

Three, the navigator's, 2026-08-17:

1. **Ship the two filters the ruleset supports and state the rest.** The list shrinks meaningfully
   today; the plan says plainly what is not filtered and why; `ah-6qp` carries the scraper work for
   dependencies and unit-type permissions. *Rejected: doing the scraper work first and narrowing
   once* — one complete bead, but it blocks a real improvement behind a scrape whose shape nobody has
   looked at, and turns this into an epic. *Rejected: dropping only the unstudiable skills* —
   narrowest and least arguable, but it leaves a maxed skill in the list.
2. **A row reads `COMB` with a dimmed `combat · 45 silver · at 3`.** Keeps the cost and adds where the
   unit already stands, so a skill being built is distinguishable from one never touched — which is
   what a STUDY list is scanned for. *Rejected: leaving the detail unchanged* (the unit pane has the
   levels, but not while you are typing); *rejected: `combat · at 3 of 5 · 45 silver`* (says the
   ceiling too, and is the longest thing in the widest popup the editor shows).
3. **A skill the unit has never studied simply omits the level** — `combat · 45 silver`. Absence is
   the message. *Rejected: `not studied`* — explicit and evenly scannable, at two words on most rows
   of a long list.

## Out of scope

- **Skill dependencies and unit-type permissions** — `ah-6qp`, filed from this bead's planning.
- **`check_studying`'s `study-at-maximum` warning.** It stays: a player can still type a maxed skill.
- **Magic-specific rules.** `SkillEntry::magic` exists but says nothing about who may study it; that
  is the same missing data `ah-6qp` covers.
- **Teachers.** A unit that could exceed a ceiling with a teacher present is not a case the ruleset's
  `max_level` describes — `max_level` is the skill's own ceiling, not the unit's circumstances, so
  nothing legitimate is hidden.
- **`GIVE`** — `ah-84w`, the sibling bead, same `match`.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Then in the application: pick a unit with a couple of skills, type `STUDY ` and press Ctrl+Space. The
list is shorter than the ruleset's ninety-six; a skill the unit has is shown with `at N`; a skill it
has maxed is absent; and nothing that cannot be studied at all is offered.

## Known traps

- **`cost: None` means "cannot be studied", not "free".** The field's doc says so and the filter
  rests on it entirely; reading it as a missing price would offer exactly the skills that can never
  be ordered.
- **Match the skill tag case-insensitively.** `check_studying` uses `eq_ignore_ascii_case` for this
  same lookup and its comment says why; a case-sensitive match here silently finds no level, so every
  skill looks unstudied and no maxed skill is ever dropped.
- **`>=` versus `>`.** A unit at `max_level` cannot study further — the same comparison
  `check_studying` makes. Off by one here either hides a legitimate skill or keeps a useless one.
- **Do not empty the list when there is no unit.** The signature promises that only the ruleset's
  presence widens the answer; a missing unit must narrow by the first filter alone.
- **Ninety-six skills is the whole point of ah-e4v**, the popup-clipping bead. This one makes the list
  shorter; it does not make a long entry readable, and the two are independent.
acceptance_criteria: Completing a skill in a STUDY order offers only skills the ordered unit is permitted to study, whose dependencies it meets, and which it has not already taken as far as it can. Whichever of those filters the ruleset cannot support is recorded rather than silently skipped. With no ruleset loaded, completion still answers sensibly.

title: GIVE completion offers what the unit holds, with the amounts
description:
Typing `GIVE 7 ` and asking for a completion offers the whole item catalogue. The module says so
outright:

> **The hex decides.** `BUY` offers what this hex has for sale, `SELL` what its market wants,
> `PRODUCE` what can be produced here — by the ground or by this unit's own skills — and `GIVE`
> and everything else offer the whole catalogue.

So the player scrolls hundreds of items to find one of the four things the unit is carrying, and the
list will happily complete something it cannot give.

**The request:** `GIVE` offers only what this unit actually holds.

## The mechanism already exists

`order_argument_completions` already takes `unit_id`, and `located(report, unit_id)` already yields
the unit and its region — that is how `BUY`, `SELL` and `PRODUCE` narrow today. A unit's items are on
the parsed unit, so this is a fourth arm of a `match` that already has three.

## Worth deciding rather than assuming

- **Amounts.** A unit holding 3 herbs can be offered `HERB`, and `GIVE 7 300 HERB` is still wrong.
  Whether the completion shows the amount held — turning the list into a manifest, which is useful in
  itself — is a decision.
- **Silver.** Held like any item, and given constantly; it should not fall out of the list by
  accident.
- **`GIVE` has other shapes.** Giving a whole unit, and `GIVE 0` to discard, take no item at all. The
  narrowing must not break the completions those need.
- **An empty inventory.** A unit holding nothing should offer nothing, which is a truthful and
  possibly startling answer — the alternative, falling back to the catalogue, is the behaviour this
  bead is removing.
design:
## Context

Typing `GIVE 7 ` and asking for a completion offers the whole item catalogue. The module says so
outright, in `crates/core/src/orders/completion.rs`'s own words:

> **The hex decides.** `BUY` offers what this hex has for sale, `SELL` what its market wants,
> `PRODUCE` what can be produced here — by the ground or by this unit's own skills — and `GIVE` and
> everything else offer the whole catalogue.

So the player scrolls hundreds of items to find one of the four things the unit is carrying, and the
list will happily complete something it cannot give. **`GIVE` offers only what the unit actually
holds.**

The mechanism is already there. `item_completions` (`completion.rs:177`) is a `match` on the order's
name with three arms, and `located(report, unit_id)` (line 200) already yields **both** the region and
the unit — `PRODUCE` uses the unit half today. This is a fourth arm reading `unit.items`.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `crates/core/src/orders/completion.rs`

**One arm and one function.** In `item_completions`, add `"GIVE"` to the guard and the match:

```rust
    if matches!(order.name, "BUY" | "SELL" | "PRODUCE" | "GIVE") {
        if let Some((region, unit)) = located(report, unit_id) {
            return match order.name {
                "BUY" => market_completions(&region.for_sale, MarketSide::Sale),
                "SELL" => market_completions(&region.wanted, MarketSide::Wanted),
                "PRODUCE" => produce_completions(region, unit, ruleset),
                "GIVE" => holdings_completions(unit),
                _ => unreachable!("guarded by the outer match"),
            };
        }
```

**The fallback comment above it stays exactly as it is** and now covers `GIVE` too: no report, no unit
id, or a unit the report does not carry means the unit cannot be found, so there is nothing to narrow
by and the catalogue stands in. That is a different case from a unit that is found and holds nothing —
see the trap about it below.

```rust
/// What the unit is carrying, as a manifest: the tag to type, and the amount beside it.
///
/// Sorted by tag like `market_completions`, so two narrowed lists read the same way. Silver is an
/// item like any other here - a report writes it `150 silver [SILV]` - so it appears without a
/// special case, which is what stops the most-given thing in the game falling out of the list.
fn holdings_completions(unit: &ReportUnit) -> Vec<OrderCompletion> {
    let mut sorted: Vec<&ItemAmount> = unit.items.iter().collect();
    sorted.sort_by(|a, b| a.tag.cmp(&b.tag));

    sorted
        .into_iter()
        .map(|item| OrderCompletion {
            value: item.tag.clone(),
            name: item.name.clone(),
            detail: format!("{} · {} held", item.name, item.amount),
        })
        .collect()
}
```

`OrderCompletion`'s three fields and the `detail` shape are `market_completions`' (line 222); follow
it rather than inventing a second format.

### Nothing else

- **No TypeScript.** `orderArgumentCompletions` renders whatever the core returns, `detail` included
  (`packages/shared/src/orderCompletion.ts`), and nothing about the shape changes.
- **No change to `located`, `market_completions`, `produce_completions` or `catalogue_completions`.**
- **No change to the other `GIVE` shapes.** Giving a whole unit (`GIVE 7 UNIT`) and discarding
  (`GIVE 0 ...`) reach `Arg::Kw`/`Arg::OneOf` positions, not `Arg::Item`, so `item_completions` is
  never called for them and they keep every keyword they offer today. The bead asks this be checked
  rather than assumed — the test named below is the check.

## Increments

One. RED: the seven tests below, in `completion.rs`'s test module. GREEN: the arm and the function.

## The test plan

| Test | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `give_offers_only_what_the_unit_holds` | A unit holding `SILV`, `HERB`, `SWOR` → those three, and no fourth catalogue entry |
| `give_names_the_amount_held` | `detail` is `herbs · 3 held`, exactly |
| `give_offers_silver_like_any_other_item` | `SILV` is in the list — the most-given thing in the game, and the one a special case would drop |
| `give_sorts_by_tag_like_a_market_list` | The same order `market_completions` produces |
| `a_unit_holding_nothing_is_offered_nothing` | Empty `items` → an empty list, **not** the catalogue. The navigator's decision |
| `give_falls_back_to_the_catalogue_when_the_unit_cannot_be_found` | No `unit_id`, or an id the report does not carry → the whole catalogue, unchanged behaviour and a different case from the one above |
| `giving_a_whole_unit_still_offers_its_keywords` | `GIVE 7 ` reaching the keyword positions (`UNIT`, `ALL`, …) is unaffected — the shapes the bead asks about |
| (existing) the `BUY`/`SELL`/`PRODUCE` narrowing tests | Unchanged |

Suites: `cargo test --workspace` and `pnpm -r run test`, inside `pnpm run check:fast`. No browser
suite: the popup's rendering is unchanged and ah-e4v is what makes it readable.

## User-facing decisions

Both the navigator's, 2026-08-17:

1. **Each row reads `HERB` with a dimmed `herbs · 3 held` beside it** — matching `BUY` and `SELL`'s
   shape exactly, and turning the list into a manifest: what the unit carries and how much, without
   leaving the order line. *Rejected: `herbs · 3`* — shorter, but a bare number sits where `BUY` puts
   a price and reads ambiguously right after looking at a market list. *Rejected: `herbs` alone* —
   narrowing is the fix and the unit pane has the amounts, but the number is free here and is the
   thing that stops `GIVE 7 300 HERB`.
2. **A unit holding nothing is offered nothing.** The popup does not appear — truthful, and possibly
   startling. *Rejected: falling back to the catalogue* — that is exactly the behaviour this bead
   removes, and it would come back precisely when it is most wrong. *Rejected: an unselectable "this
   unit holds nothing" row* — it explains the silence, at the cost of a kind of entry the completion
   list has never had.

## Out of scope

- **Validating the amount.** `GIVE 7 300 HERB` from a unit holding 3 is still writable; the detail
  says `3 held`, and the order checks are what refuse it. Narrowing the *items* is this bead.
- **ah-3ej**, the same idea for `STUDY` and skills. Sibling bead, same `match`, planned separately.
- **`GIVE`'s other shapes** — beyond the test that proves they still work.
- **Shared stock.** A unit can give what the hex's sharing units hold, which is not on this unit's
  `items`. Deliberately not offered: the completion says what *this* unit carries, which is what the
  bead asked for, and a shared-stock list would need the pooling rules `semantics.rs` owns. Worth a
  bead if it ever bites.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Then in the application: select a unit with a short inventory, type `GIVE 7 ` and press Ctrl+Space —
only what it holds, each with its amount. Then try it on a unit holding nothing: no popup. Then
`GIVE 7 U` and check `UNIT` is still offered.

## Known traps

- **"Holds nothing" and "cannot be found" are different, and only one falls back.** A unit the report
  does not carry keeps the catalogue (`located` returns `None`, the existing comment explains why); a
  unit that *is* found and holds nothing returns an empty list. Writing one test and not the other
  leaves the wrong one silently wrong.
- **Silver is an item.** A report writes `150 silver [SILV]` in a unit's line, so it arrives in
  `unit.items` and needs no special case — but it is the thing most often given, so if it is missing
  from the list something has filtered it and the test above is what catches that.
- **`item_completions` is reached only from an `Arg::Item` position.** Do not add narrowing anywhere
  in `completions_for`'s keyword arm; `GIVE`'s `UNIT` and `ALL` live there and are not items.
- **Follow `market_completions`' `detail` format.** Two narrowed lists that read differently is the
  kind of drift this repository files refactoring beads about.
acceptance_criteria: Completing an item in a GIVE order offers only items the ordered unit holds, in the same way BUY and SELL already narrow to the hex. Other shapes of GIVE, including giving a unit and discarding with GIVE 0, still complete as they do today. A unit holding nothing offers no items rather than the whole catalogue.

title: Order OCD: a setting that uppercases order keywords
description:
Orders are case-insensitive to the engine, so a turn written in lower case runs exactly as one
shouted in capitals. Some players like the keywords uppercase anyway — it separates the commands from
the names and reads like the manual — and doing it by hand is tedious and easy to miss.

**The request:** a setting, **Order OCD**, that uppercases every keyword in the orders.

Suggested description for the setting: *"Uppercase the command keywords as you write, so MOVE, STUDY
and ALL stand out from names. Text inside quotes is left alone."*

## The rule that makes it safe

**Nothing inside quotation marks is touched.** Unit names, faction names and structure names are
quoted precisely because they are arbitrary text, and uppercasing `"Seven of Eight"` changes data
rather than presentation. That is the one hard requirement in this bead — the rest is taste.

The keyword list already exists: `order_commands` is exported from the core and is what the editor's
command completion is built from, so "what is a keyword" needs no new judgement. Note that argument
keywords are keywords too — `ALL`, `SILV`, item and direction tags — and whether they are in scope is
a decision, not an oversight. The setting's name suggests the player wants all of them.

## For the planner to settle with the navigator

- **When it happens.** As you type, on leaving a line, on save, or as an explicit "tidy these orders"
  action. Uppercasing mid-word while somebody types is a well-known way to make an editor feel
  possessed, and this is the decision the whole feel of the feature rests on.
- **How far it reaches.** Commands only, or arguments and tags as well.
- **Whether it rewrites what is already there** when switched on, or only what is typed afterwards.
- **Global or per game.** The settings widget has both, and this is a personal-taste setting rather
  than a property of a game.

## Validation

With the setting on, typing a command in lower case leaves it uppercase, and a quoted name typed in
mixed case is untouched — including a quoted name containing a word that is also a keyword. With the
setting off, nothing changes. Orders already written are handled however the navigator decided,
consistently.
acceptance_criteria: A setting called Order OCD, with a short description of what it does, uppercases the command keywords in orders when enabled and changes nothing when disabled. Text inside quotation marks is never altered, including quoted names that contain keywords.
close_reason: All children closed; last was ah-bn6.2, delivered in PR #416

title: The not-traded-here warning uses a hyphen, like every other core message
description:
Found while verifying ah-d8u (Psylocke, 2026-08-17, origin/main 0ed5814). Not a defect in what the check does - the warning fires correctly and the navigator passed the bead - but a one-character inconsistency worth tidying.

crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:538 builds the not-traded-here message with an em dash:

    "this hex does not {verb} {name} — its market {has_or_wants} {}"

It is the only player-facing string in that file with a non-ASCII character. Every other message is ASCII, and ah-djq's own design notes state the convention outright: 'Messages are ASCII in this codebase - twelve of twelve. The em dash in the mockup is a hyphen in the code.'

The cost being paid: a reader of the file cannot tell which convention holds, and the next message copied from a mockup will copy whichever example it happens to land on. A player on a terminal or a font without the glyph sees a replacement character in one warning and not the others.

The change is one character at :538 plus the four test strings that pin the same message (:3189, :3213, :3230, :3342). Whether the fix is a hyphen or the convention should change instead is the navigator's call at triage - the point is that the file should say one thing.
design:
## Context

Found by Psylocke while verifying ah-d8u (2026-08-17, origin/main 0ed5814). Not a defect — the check
fires correctly and the bead passed verification — but the message it emits is the only player-facing
string in `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs` that is not ASCII:

```rust
// crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs
"this hex does not {verb} {name} — its market {has_or_wants} {}",
```

The other twelve messages in that file use a plain hyphen, and ah-djq's own design notes state the
convention outright: *"Messages are ASCII in this codebase - twelve of twelve. The em dash in the
mockup is a hyphen in the code."* So the file says two things, and the next message copied from a
mockup will copy whichever example its author happens to land on.

**One argument in the bead does not hold, and the plan should not repeat it.** It says a player on a
terminal or a font without the glyph sees a replacement character. This application has no terminal
UI — both shells are browser-based — so nobody ever sees a replacement glyph. The reason to do this is
consistency inside the core, and nothing else. The navigator was told that before ranking it, and
ranked it P3 anyway.

After this bead, `grep -P '[^\x00-\x7F]'` over that file returns doc comments only.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs` — one character, and the tests that pin it

**Do not work from line numbers — this file moves under you.** It has changed three times today
(ah-dbb.2, ah-j0e), and the numbers in the bead itself are already wrong. Find every occurrence by the
character:

```bash
grep -nP '[^\x00-\x7F]' crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs
```

At `ec82563` that is eight hits: the message (538), **five test strings** (3259, 3283, 3300, and the
two continuation lines 3412 and 3414), and two doc comments (1494, 2552) that stay. Expect the
numbers to have moved again by the time you run it; the shape of the answer will not have.

| String |
|---|
| `"this hex does not {verb} {name} — its market {has_or_wants} {}"` — **the message** |
| `"this hex does not sell silk — its market has perfume and gems"` |
| `"this hex does not want fur — its market wants grain and livestock"` |
| `"this hex does not sell silk — its market has perfume"` |
| `"this hex does not sell silk — its market has perfume, gems, hill dwarves and \` |
| `"this hex does not want fur — its market wants grain, livestock, fish, spears, \` |

Five test strings, not the four the bead names — the two continuation lines are easy to miss because
the dash is not on the line the assertion
starts on.

**The two remaining non-ASCII hits in the file are doc comments** (one on `check_forms`, one on the
sharing flag). They ship to no player and read better as they are. Leave them, and
say so in the commit message so the next reader of `grep` output is not surprised.

### Nothing else

- **No TypeScript.** The message is built in the core and rendered as given; nothing in `packages/`
  asserts on it (`grep -rn "does not sell" packages` is empty).
- **No smoke test.** `grep -rn "does not sell\|does not want" tests/` is empty.
- **`docs/ui/buy-not-for-sale.html`** shows an *earlier* wording of this message ("does not sell
  grain: it offers wood elves and leaders") from ah-d8u's design conversation. It is a record of what
  the navigator was shown, not a copy of the shipped string — do not edit it.
- **`docs/order-checks/README.md`** uses em dashes throughout, in prose. Not a message; leave it.

## Increments

One.

RED: change the five test strings first; the suite fails against the em dash still in the message.
GREEN: the message itself.

Doing it in that order is the point — it is the only thing that proves the five tests actually pin
the character, rather than five strings being edited to match whatever the code now says.

## The test plan

No new tests. The five existing assertions listed above are the whole net, and after this bead they
pin the hyphen.

One check that is not a test, and is worth running by hand because it is the bead's actual acceptance
criterion:

```bash
grep -nP '[^\x00-\x7F]' crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs
```

Two hits, both doc comments. No string literal.

Suites: `cargo test --workspace`, inside `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

The message is a string the player reads, so the direction was the navigator's, taken 2026-08-17:

> **Hyphen — match the other twelve.** `this hex does not sell silk - its market has perfume`

*Rejected: moving all thirteen core messages to em dashes* to match the TypeScript UI, which already
uses `—`, `→` and `←` freely — typographically better and closer to how the app reads, but a wider
diff and thirteen messages' tests for a change nobody asked for. *Rejected: closing the bead as not
worth doing.*

No other wording changes: the verb, the market list and the order of the clauses all stay exactly as
they are.

## Out of scope

- **The TypeScript side's punctuation.** `packages/shared/src/workspace/` uses non-ASCII deliberately
  and often (`→ ocean (49,33)`, `+1 merged`, `—` for an empty cell). This bead is about the Rust core's
  own convention and touches no shell string.
- **Writing the convention down somewhere.** Tempting, and a different bead: the place for it would be
  a comment at the top of `semantics.rs` or a line in `docs/`, and choosing which is not a
  one-character change.
- **The two doc comments** that also use an em dash.
- **The mockup and the order-checks README.**

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
grep -nP '[^\x00-\x7F]' crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs   # doc comments only
```

Nothing for a person to look at: the message renders the same width in the same place, with one
character changed. Psylocke can mark it as touching nothing worth a verification pass.

## Known traps

- **An em dash and a hyphen look alike in a diff.** Do not eyeball it — the `grep -P` above is the
  check, and it belongs in the PR body.
- **Two of the five test strings continue onto the next line**, so a search that looks
  only at the line an assertion begins on misses them. Search the file for the character, not for the
  sentence.
- **Change the tests first.** If the message is fixed first, all five tests are then edited to agree
  with the code and nothing has been proved.
- **Do not reformat the surrounding strings.** `cargo fmt --check` runs in `check:fast`, and a
  re-wrapped multi-line string literal turns a one-character bead into a diff nobody can read.

title: The ruleset carries the buildings and how many mages each seats
description:
Second prerequisite for ah-a2k.2, filed 2026-08-17 after the navigator chose the fuller scope for that check (mockup .cerebro/scratch/ah-a2k.2-magic-study.html, question 1, option B).

## Why it exists

ah-a2k.2 warns a mage whose magic study above level 2 is halved for want of a building to study in.
The rules are explicit that not every building helps -- 'Mages is the number of mages that the
building provides study facilities for, to enable unhindered study above level 2 in magical skills'
(tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html:3248). The navigator was offered a narrower check that
warns only when the mage stands outside every structure, which needs no new data and catches all
five corpus cases, and chose this instead.

**The client has no building data at all.** config/public/ruleset.json carries exactly gaps, items,
movement, risk, skills and source; its items are only equipment, man, monster, mount and ship. There
is no structure anywhere in the ruleset or in crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs.

## The source, which is clean and already committed

A real HTML table at tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html:3136, six rows including its
header:

    (name) | Size | Cost | Material | Skill (min level) | Mages
    Tower     | 10   | 10   | stone    | building (1)      | 0
    Fort      | 50   | 40   | stone    | building (1)      | 1
    Castle    | 300  | 300  | stone    | building (2)      | 2
    Citadel   | 1000 | 800  | stone    | building (3)      | 3
    Stockade  | 50   | 60   | wood     | building (1)      | 1

**Note the Tower seats zero mages.** The obvious assumption -- that a Tower is where a mage studies
-- is wrong in this ruleset, and it is exactly the mistake ah-a2k.2 will catch. Any test written for
this bead should pin it.

The header row's first cell is blank in the source; the building's name is the first column.

## What this bead delivers

Building data scraped by packages/ruleset from that table, carried in config/public/ruleset.json,
and exposed on the Rust Ruleset the way items and skills already are -- at minimum each building's
name and its mage capacity, and whatever else of Size/Cost/Material/Skill comes free from parsing
the same row. An accessor in the shape of Ruleset::is_man (crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:574)
answering 'how many mages may study in a structure of this kind', with None for a kind the table
does not list.

Matching a report's structure to a table row is part of this bead: the report writes
'+ Tower [5] : Tower.' and '+ Building [2] : Road SE.', so the kind as printed has to be matched
against the table's names, and everything unmatched -- Mine, Quarry, Inn, Road, ships -- seats no
mages.

## Open for this bead's planning session

Whether to model buildings as a new top-level ruleset key or to widen items with a building kind;
how much of the row to carry beyond the mage capacity; and how a partly built structure ('needs 4')
is treated. None of these is user-facing.

## What it must not do

Guess. A structure kind the table does not name is not evidence of anything, and ah-a2k.2 must be
able to tell 'seats no mages' from 'cannot say' -- see that bead's accept-on-doubt requirement.
design:
## Context

`ah-a2k.2` warns a mage whose magic study above level 2 is halved for want of a building to study
in. The rules are explicit that not every building helps:

> "Mages is the number of mages that the building provides study facilities for, to enable
> unhindered study above level 2 in magical skills."
> — `tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html:3248`

**The client has no building data at all.** `config/public/ruleset.json` carries exactly `gaps`,
`items`, `movement`, `risk`, `skills`, `source`, and its `items` are only `equipment`, `man`,
`monster`, `mount` and `ship`. `Ruleset` (`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:318-328`) has no
structures either.

The navigator was offered a narrower `ah-a2k.2` that warns only when the mage stands outside every
structure — which needs nothing new and catches all five corpus cases — and chose the fuller answer
instead (2026-08-17). This bead is the data that makes it possible, and nothing else.

**The source is a clean HTML table**, already committed, at
`tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html:3136`:

| (name) | Size | Cost | Material | Skill (min level) | Mages |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tower | 10 | 10 | stone | building (1) | **0** |
| Fort | 50 | 40 | stone | building (1) | **1** |
| Castle | 300 | 300 | stone | building (2) | **2** |
| Citadel | 1000 | 800 | stone | building (3) | **3** |
| Stockade | 50 | 60 | wood | building (1) | **1** |

Six `<tr>` rows including the header, whose first cell is blank — the building's name is the first
column of each body row.

**A Tower seats zero mages, and that is the point.** The obvious assumption — a Tower is where a
mage studies — is wrong in this ruleset, and it is exactly the mistake `ah-a2k.2` exists to catch.
Pin it in a test so nobody "corrects" it.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

Line numbers are against `origin/main` at `da795b1`. `ah-a2k.1` touches `data.ts`, the committed
ruleset and `rules.rs` too, so if it has landed the numbers will have moved a little; the named
functions have not.

### `packages/ruleset/src/html.ts` — a table reader, the first one

`htmlToText` (`:36`) flattens a page to one run of text and `preformattedText` (`:52`) returns the
`<pre>` blocks. Neither preserves a table's structure, and the module's own header says it is "just
enough HTML handling for two engine-generated pages". This adds the third thing those pages need.

```ts
/**
 * The rows of the first table whose header names every column given, as cells of decoded text.
 *
 * The rules page states the buildings as a table and nothing else in it needs one, so this looks a
 * table up by what its header says rather than by position - a page that grows another table above
 * this one should not silently return that one instead. Empty cells are kept, because the buildings
 * table's header leaves its first cell blank and the column positions have to line up.
 */
export function tableRows(html: string, headings: string[]): string[][]
```

Implementation notes, so this is one reading and not two:

- Match `<table[^>]*>[\s\S]*?<\/table>` with the `g` flag, take each candidate, split it on
  `<tr[^>]*>[\s\S]*?<\/tr>`, and split each row on `<t[dh][^>]*>[\s\S]*?<\/t[dh]>`.
- Run each cell's inner text through the same decoding `htmlToText` uses — export the private
  `decodeEntities` (`:18`), or factor a small `cellText` beside it, rather than copying the entity
  map.
- A table qualifies when its **first** row contains every string in `headings`, compared
  case-insensitively after trimming. Return the remaining rows.
- Return `[]` when no table qualifies. The caller, not this function, decides that is fatal.

Tests go in a **new** `packages/ruleset/src/html.test.ts` — there is none today: a two-column
table found by its headings; a page with two tables where the second is the match; a page with none
giving `[]`; and a row whose cells contain `<a href>` links and `&` coming back as clean text.

### `packages/ruleset/src/rules.ts` — parsing the buildings

`rules.ts` reads the rules page and today exports only `parseMovementRules` (`:155`) over prose.
`rules.ts` already imports `htmlToText` from `./html` (`:12`) — add `tableRows` to that import.
It also *defines* `RulesetScrapeError` itself (`:93`), so throwing one needs no import. Add beside
`parseMovementRules`:

```ts
/** A building the rules table describes, and how many mages may study in it. */
export type BuildingEntry = {
  name: string;
  /** People it shelters. */
  size: number;
  /** Man-months of labour, and units of material, to finish it. */
  cost: number;
  /** What it is built from, as the table words it: `stone`, `wood`. */
  material: string;
  /**
   * How many mages the building provides study facilities for, "to enable unhindered study above
   * level 2 in magical skills". **Zero for a Tower** - the obvious guess is wrong in this ruleset,
   * and a mage studying in one loses half the month.
   */
  mages: number;
};

export type BuildingReference = Record<string, BuildingEntry>;

export function parseBuildings(html: string): BuildingReference
```

keyed by the building's name **uppercased**, so a report's printed kind can be matched without
caring about case — `items` and `skills` are both keyed by their uppercase tag
(`config/public/ruleset.json`, checked: zero of 96 skill keys differ from their `tag`), and this
follows that.

`parseBuildings` calls `tableRows(html, ["Size", "Cost", "Material", "Mages"])` — four headings that
identify the table without depending on the exact wording of `Skill (min level)`, which is the cell
most likely to be reworded. It reads name from cell 0, then `Size`, `Cost`, `Material`, `Mages` by
their **header position** rather than by a fixed index, so a column inserted in the middle does not
silently shift the mage count.

Throw `RulesetScrapeError` when the table is missing or yields no rows, in the style of
`parseSkillReference`'s own guard (`data.ts:474-480`) — the message should say what shape was
expected and that the page has probably changed. A ruleset that cannot say which buildings seat
mages must fail the scrape rather than quietly produce none, because `ah-a2k.2` cannot tell
"no buildings" from "seats nobody".

### `packages/ruleset/src/build.ts` — assembling it

`buildRuleset` (`:99`) already calls `parseMovementRules(input.rulesHtml)` and the two data-page
parsers, with a sanity floor after the items (`:108-114`). Add `parseBuildings(input.rulesHtml)`
after the movement parse — it reads the same page — and put `buildings` into the returned object.
Its `Ruleset` type in the same file gains `buildings: BuildingReference`.

Order the new key in the emitted JSON as the existing ones are ordered; `committed.test.ts` compares
the whole object, so a differently ordered key is a diff to look at rather than a failure, but keep
it tidy.

### `config/public/ruleset.json` — regenerated, never hand-edited

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape -- \
  --rules tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html \
  --data tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html
```

That is the command `packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts:12-14` prints when it fails, and that
test will fail until it is run. The diff should add one `buildings` object with five entries and
change nothing else.

### `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs` — the core side

```rust
/// A building the rules describe, and how many mages may study in it.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct BuildingEntry {
    pub name: String,
    pub size: i64,
    pub cost: i64,
    pub material: String,
    /// How many mages the building provides study facilities for. **Zero for a Tower**, which is
    /// the ruleset's own answer and not an oversight: a mage studying in one gets half a month.
    pub mages: i64,
}
```

and on `Ruleset` (`:318-328`):

```rust
    /// Empty for a ruleset generated before buildings were scraped. Empty means nothing can be
    /// said about a structure, not that no structure seats a mage.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub buildings: BTreeMap<String, BuildingEntry>,
```

**`#[serde(default)]` is not optional here, and neither is adding the field at all.** `Ruleset`
carries `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]` (`:316-317`), so the two sides
must move together: a regenerated JSON with `buildings` against a core that does not know the field
fails to parse *the whole ruleset*, not just the new part. And without `default`, a ruleset a user
cached before this bead stops loading. `skills` already carries `default` for the same reason
(`:326`).

Beside `is_man` (`:574`):

```rust
    /// How many mages may study unhindered in a structure of this kind, when the catalogue knows
    /// the kind at all.
    ///
    /// `None` for a structure the rules' buildings table does not name - a Mine, an Inn, a road, a
    /// ship - and for a ruleset scraped before buildings were. That is deliberately distinct from
    /// `Some(0)`, which is a Tower: one says the catalogue cannot tell you, the other says the
    /// building seats nobody, and a caller that must not guess needs to tell them apart.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn mage_capacity(&self, kind: &str) -> Option<i64> {
        self.buildings
            .get(&kind.to_ascii_uppercase())
            .map(|building| building.mages)
    }
```

**Matching a report's structure kind is this accessor's job and is the subtle part.** The report
writes `+ Tower [5] : Tower.` and `+ Building [2] : Road SE.`, so `Structure.kind` is the word after
the colon — `Tower`, `Road SE`, `Longship`. Uppercasing and looking up handles `Tower`; everything
else misses and returns `None`, which is right. Do **not** try to strip a trailing direction or
match a prefix: `Road SE` is not a building in the table and must not resolve to one.

### Nothing else

No advisory code, no settings entry, no vocabulary regeneration, no TypeScript outside
`packages/ruleset`. `ah-a2k.2` is the first and only caller of `mage_capacity`.

## Increments

**1 — A table can be read.** RED: the `html.test.ts` cases. GREEN by `tableRows`.

**2 — The buildings parse.** RED: `rules.test.ts` asserting `parseBuildings(RULES_HTML)["TOWER"]`
is `{ name: "Tower", size: 10, cost: 10, material: "stone", mages: 0 }` and `["CITADEL"].mages`
is 3. GREEN by `parseBuildings`.

**3 — The scrape carries them.** RED: `committed.test.ts` fails, because `buildRuleset` now emits a
key the committed file lacks. GREEN by wiring it into `buildRuleset` and running the scrape.
`pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test`.

**4 — The core reads them.** RED: the Rust tests below. GREEN by `BuildingEntry`, the `Ruleset`
field and `mage_capacity`. `cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core`.

**5 — Gate.** `pnpm run check:fast`.

## The test plan

### `packages/ruleset/src/html.test.ts`

`tableRows` found by headings; the second of two tables chosen when only it matches; `[]` when none
matches; a row with `<a href>` and `&` decoded to clean text; a header row with a blank first
cell still yielding rows whose first cell is the name.

### `packages/ruleset/src/rules.test.ts`

- `the_buildings_table_is_read` — all five, by name and mage count.
- `a_tower_seats_no_mages` — its own test, with a comment saying this is the ruleset's answer and
  not a mistake. **This is the test that stops somebody "fixing" it.**
- `a_page_without_the_table_is_refused` — `parseBuildings("<html></html>")` throws
  `RulesetScrapeError`.
- `columns_are_found_by_their_heading` — a hand-built table with an extra column inserted between
  `Material` and `Mages` still reads the mage count correctly. This is what the
  position-by-heading rule buys, and without a test nothing holds it.

### `packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts`

A census, in the shape of `ah-a2k.1`'s:

```ts
  it("carries the five buildings and what each seats", () => {
    expect(
      Object.values(COMMITTED.buildings).map((b) => [b.name, b.mages])
    ).toEqual([
      ["Castle", 2], ["Citadel", 3], ["Fort", 1], ["Stockade", 1], ["Tower", 0]
    ]);
  });
```

Check the iteration order before asserting it — the emitted object's key order follows how
`parseBuildings` inserts, so either sort in the test or match the insertion order. Sorting is safer.

### `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs` tests

- `a_buildings_mage_capacity_is_known` — `mage_capacity("Tower")` is `Some(0)`,
  `mage_capacity("Citadel")` is `Some(3)`, `mage_capacity("tower")` is `Some(0)` (case), and
  `mage_capacity("Road SE")` is `None`.
- `a_structure_the_table_does_not_name_is_unknown_not_zero` — its own test, asserting `None` rather
  than `Some(0)` for `"Mine"`. The distinction is the whole reason the return type is an `Option`.
- `a_ruleset_without_buildings_still_parses` — `Ruleset::from_json` over a small JSON with no
  `buildings` key succeeds and `mage_capacity` answers `None`. This is what `#[serde(default)]`
  buys.

### Everything else stays green

`pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test`, `cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core`, `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

**None.** This bead adds a table to a scraped data file, a Rust type and one accessor. Nothing a
player sees changes. The decision that produced it — that `ah-a2k.2` should tell a study building
from an ordinary one rather than only noticing a mage standing outside everything — was the
navigator's, taken on 2026-08-17 against
`.cerebro/scratch/ah-a2k.2-magic-study.html`, and is recorded in `ah-a2k.2`'s notes along with the
correction that a Tower seats zero.

## Out of scope

- **The check**, which is `ah-a2k.2`, blocked by this bead and by `ah-a2k.1`.
- **Whether a building is finished.** The report writes `needs 4` for an unfinished one
  (`Structure.needs`); whether an unfinished Castle seats its mages is `ah-a2k.2`'s question, and
  this bead only says what a finished one seats.
- **How many mages are already inside.** A Fort seats one; two mages in it means one is unhoused.
  That is `ah-a2k.2` counting units, not data this bead supplies.
- **Structures that are not in this table** — Mines, Quarries, Inns, roads, ships. They seat no
  mages, and `mage_capacity` says `None` for them, which is the honest answer.
- **The production bonuses** other structures give (`neworigins-rules.html:3253-3266`). A different
  table and a different bead; nobody has filed one.
- **Anything else building data could serve** — a build planner, a shelter check. This adds a table
  and one accessor.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape -- \
  --rules tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html \
  --data tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core
pnpm run check:fast
```

**Look once, at the diff.** Nothing here shows in the shell:

```bash
git diff --stat config/public/ruleset.json
jq -r '.buildings | to_entries[] | "\(.key)  mages=\(.value.mages)  size=\(.value.size)"' config/public/ruleset.json
```

The second should print exactly five lines, with `TOWER mages=0`, `FORT mages=1`,
`CASTLE mages=2`, `CITADEL mages=3`, `STOCKADE mages=1`. Then check the diff adds only the
`buildings` key — no movement in `source`, `items`, `skills`, `movement`, `risk` or `gaps`.

## Known traps

- **`Ruleset` is `deny_unknown_fields`** (`rules.rs:316-317`). The JSON and the Rust struct must
  change together: regenerating the ruleset without adding the field makes the *whole* ruleset fail
  to parse, and every check that needs it goes silent at once. If the shell suddenly stops pricing
  anything, this is why.
- **`#[serde(default)]` on the new field**, or a ruleset cached before this bead stops loading.
- **A Tower seats zero mages.** Two tests exist to stop it being "fixed". It is the ruleset's answer
  and the reason `ah-a2k.2` is worth building.
- **`None` and `Some(0)` mean different things.** A Mine is `None` — the catalogue cannot say. A
  Tower is `Some(0)` — it seats nobody. Collapsing them would make `ah-a2k.2` warn about a mage in a
  Mine on the same evidence as a mage in a Tower, and only one of those is knowable.
- **Match the structure kind exactly.** `Road SE` must not resolve to anything by prefix or by
  stripping a direction. Uppercase and look up; a miss is the right answer.
- **Find the columns by their heading, not by index.** The table's header leaves its first cell
  blank, so a naive zero-based read is already off by one for every column, and a column added
  later would shift the mage count silently.
- **`committed.test.ts` fails until the ruleset is regenerated**, and prints the exact command.
  Never hand-edit `config/public/ruleset.json`.
- **`ah-a2k.1` touches the same three files** (`data.ts`, the committed ruleset, `rules.rs`) and may
  land first or second. Expect a small conflict in `config/public/ruleset.json` — regenerate rather
  than resolving it by hand.
acceptance_criteria: Given the committed ruleset, the core can answer how many mages a structure of a given kind seats. Tower is 0, Fort and Stockade 1, Castle 2, Citadel 3, and a kind the table does not name is not-known rather than zero. The classification is pinned by a test, including the Tower-seats-zero case. The scrape is reproducible with pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape and committed.test.ts passes.

title: Warn when a mage above level 2 studies magic outside a building that houses mages
description:
Split out of ah-a2k on 2026-08-17. The check itself; ah-a2k.1 supplies the one fact it cannot get today.

## Evidence
'Warning: Magic study rate outside of a building cut in half above level 2.' - 5 occurrences across
2 turns of 2 games (docs/order-checks/corpus-errors.generated.md). The month's study still happens;
half of it is wasted. The engine's own message is advisory rather than a refusal, so this check
mirrors an advisory and not a rejection.

## What it needs
- **Is the studied skill magic?** ah-a2k.1, which blocks this bead. Nothing in the client can answer
  it today - see that bead for why cast is not a proxy.
- **The unit's current level in that skill.** ReportUnit.skills carries Skill { tag, level, .. };
  the threshold is level 2, so a unit at level 2 or above studying to 3 is the case. Confirm from
  the rules whether the halving applies at the level being studied *to* or *from* before writing the
  comparison - the message says 'above level 2' and the exact boundary has not been checked.
- **Is the unit inside a building?** ReportUnit.structure_id names the structure it stands in, and
  the region's structures carry kind. A **fleet is not a building**:
  movement::mode::parse_fleet_kind(kind) already tells them apart and returns Some for a hull or a
  'Fleet, N Corsairs'. Whether every non-fleet structure counts as a building for this rule, and
  whether an unfinished one does, is this bead's planning session to settle from the rules.
- **The STUDY intent's skill**, already read as Intent::Study { skill } and resolved by
  Ruleset::find_skill.

## What it must not do
Never blocking. Accept on doubt: if the ruleset cannot say whether the skill is magic, or the report
cannot say whether the unit is inside a building, stay silent
(crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:1-17).

## Shape to copy
check_teaching and check_sailing in crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs: iterate hex.units, find the
STUDY placement, emit through Ordered::finding so the warning lands on the STUDY line. A new code in
codes::ALL, a regenerated coreVocabulary.generated.ts, and an entry in the Orders group of
WARNING_GROUPS (packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.tsx).

## Validation
A level-3-or-above magic skill studied outside a building warns. The same study inside a building,
or a non-magic skill at any level, stays silent.
design:
## Context

Second child of ah-a2k, and the one that does the work. Its two prerequisites shipped this morning
and are both on main:

- **ah-a2k.1** (53be3f7) — `Ruleset::is_magic(tag)` (`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:609`), from a
  `magic: bool` on each skill.
- **ah-a2k.3** (8a24ece) — `Ruleset::mage_capacity(kind)`
  (`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:621`), from the rules' buildings table. `Some(0)` for a Tower —
  which seats no mages, and is the case this bead exists to catch — `Some(1)` Fort, `Some(2)` Castle,
  `Some(3)` Citadel, and `None` for a kind the table does not name (a Mine, an Inn, a road, a ship)
  **and** for a ruleset cached before buildings were scraped.

The engine says, advisorily: *"Magic study rate outside of a building cut in half above level 2."*
Five occurrences across two turns of two games in the committed corpus
(`docs/order-checks/corpus-errors.generated.md`). The month's study still happens; half of it is
wasted, and the player finds out a turn later.

"Above level 2" means the level being reached is 3 or more — so the unit's **current** level in that
skill is 2 or above. A unit at level 1 studying to 2 is unaffected.

The check mirrors an advisory, never a refusal, and it is never blocking.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

`check_studying` (`crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:1393`) is the template: same iteration over
`hex.units`, same `studies_placed()`, same `find_skill`, same level lookup. Copy its shape rather
than inventing another.

### `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs`

One accessor, because "the ruleset knows no buildings at all" and "this kind is not in the table" both
read as `None` from `mage_capacity`, and only the first means *stay silent*:

```rust
/// Whether this ruleset carries the buildings table at all.
///
/// `mage_capacity` answers `None` both for a kind the table does not name and for a ruleset cached
/// before ah-a2k.3 scraped the table - a Mine really has no mage seats, but a ruleset that knows no
/// buildings knows nothing about any of them, and a check that cannot tell those apart would warn
/// about every unit in the game.
#[must_use]
pub fn knows_buildings(&self) -> bool {
    !self.buildings.is_empty()
}
```

### `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs`

A new code beside `STUDY_AT_MAXIMUM` (line 93), and in `codes::ALL` (line 104, which becomes
`[Code; 20]`) — **at the end of the array**, since `ADVISORY_CHECK_CODES` is generated "in that
order" and appending keeps the existing order stable:

```rust
    pub const MAGIC_STUDY_OUTSIDE_BUILDING: Code = Code("magic-study-outside-building");
```

A new check, called from the dispatch beside its neighbours (line 225, immediately after
`check_studying`):

```rust
/// Magic studied above level 2 where nothing houses the mage: half the month is wasted.
///
/// The engine's own message is advisory - the study happens, at half rate - so this mirrors an
/// advisory and never a refusal.
///
/// Silent when the ruleset cannot say: no ruleset, no buildings table, a skill the catalogue does
/// not know, or a unit standing in a structure this region's report does not list. Not silent for
/// an unfinished building: the navigator settled that one (2026-08-17) - an unfinished building
/// shelters nobody, so the study is halved and the player is told.
fn check_magic_study(
    hex: &Hex<'_>,
    ruleset: Option<&Ruleset>,
    options: &CheckOptions,
    findings: &mut Vec<Finding>,
)
```

The body, decision by decision:

1. `let Some(ruleset) = ruleset else { return };` and
   `if !ruleset.knows_buildings() { return; }` and
